newsitem.title: USA: Medical marijuana supporters join research debate.
newsitem.headline: Medical marijuana supporters join research debate.

text.p: A homemade bamboo pipe and a set of handcuffs were on display on Thursday at a public forum on the future of U.S. research into the medical use of marijuana.

"I'm in a wheelchair already; do you want to see me in jail?" Andrew Hassenfeld, who said he smoked marijuana to ease the muscle tension of multiple sclerosis, asked an expert panel at the National Institutes of Health.

The spirited but civil public comment session came on the last day of a two-day workshop aimed at exploring what is known and what must be learned about marijuana's possible benefit for people with AIDS, cancer, glaucoma, multiple sclerosis and other serious diseases.
Chuck Thomas of the Washington-based Marijuana Policy Project held up a pair of handcuffs and said: "Right now this is the government's health care programme for medical marijuana."
Another speaker, David Goldstein, displayed a bamboo pipe he said he had made that enabled him to take marijuana easily.

Medical use of marijuana has been studied and discussed for decades, but the debate has gained new prominence since voters in Arizona and California last November approved initiatives to make it available to patients.
The Clinton administration responded quickly, threatening to penalise doctors who incorporate marijuana in their practices. Under federal law, marijuana is illegal and has no approved clinical use.

"This issue need not be so political, but if the Clinton administration uses these calls for more research to simply drag its feet on access for patients and access for researchers, you're going to hear a lot more contentiousness from our side," a man identified only as Fratella told the committee.

Other speakers asked questions about bureaucratic cooperation between state and federal health agencies, and about the procedure for obtaining NIH funding for any potential studies of medical marijuana.

The conference, held under the auspices of the NIH National Institute on Drug Abuse, was convened to focus on the state of scientific research into marijuana, according to the drug institute's director, Dr. Alan Leshner.

In Wednesday's session, the expert panel discussed some of the difficulties in conducting clinical trials. They will probably take a month or so to complete recommendations on what type of marijuana-related research NIH might conduct or support.

Some studies have shown marijuana can help control nausea in cancer patients and some doctors believe the drug can give significant relief to terminally ill patients. But other doctors argue newly available drugs do a better job than marijuana of controlling the nausea and vomiting caused by chemotherapy.

A synthetic form of THC, the active ingredient in marijuana, can be prescribed legally in pill form for cancer and AIDS patients who suffer from "wasting syndrome" in which they lose dangerous amounts of weight.
But not all patients do well on the synthetic drug, and several studies have found that patients reported more relief when they smoked marijuana.
